# Generalised additive mixed models

<style>
  :root {
    --footer-text:  "Generalised additive mixed models";
    --qr:           `r qr_css`;
    --lecture:      `r lecture_label`;
  }
</style>

::: {.fact}
`Did you know:` Egyptian fruit bats live in colonies of hundreds to thousands of individuals, can live for at least 25 years in captivity, and are extremely [vocal]{.hl} in their social interactions.

_Source: Prat, Taub & Yovel (2015), Science Advances_
:::

## Where we are

Last time: smooth terms, difference smooths and significance testing with GAMs, in models that treated every measurement as independent. Today: the "mixed" part, following the second half of Sóskuthy's (2018) workshop.

## Today

1. Dependencies in curve data
2. Random effects in GAMMs
3. Autocorrelation
4. Non-linear interactions
5. Checking and reporting

## The data {.smaller}

The PRICE trajectories from lecture 4, now with an ordered factor for L1.

```{r}
set.seed(2029)
speakers <- tibble(speaker = sprintf("S%02d", 1:20),
                   l1 = rep(c("English", "Italian"), each = 10),
                   s0 = rnorm(20, 0, 60),
                   s_mid = rnorm(20, 0, 5))
tokens <- crossing(speakers, token = 1:10) |>
  mutate(traj = paste(speaker, token, sep = "."),
         duration = round(runif(n(), 120, 300)),
         t0 = rnorm(n(), 0, 40))
price <- crossing(tokens, time = seq(0, 100, by = 10)) |>
  arrange(traj, time) |>
  mutate(onset = if_else(l1 == "English", 1250, 1320),
         offset = if_else(l1 == "English", 2050, 1900) - 2 * (250 - duration),
         mid = if_else(l1 == "English", 62, 50) + s_mid,
         width = if_else(l1 == "English", 8, 14),
         f2 = onset + (offset - onset) * plogis((time - mid) / width) + s0 + t0) |>
  group_by(traj) |>
  mutate(f2 = round(f2 + as.numeric(arima.sim(list(ar = 0.6), n = n(), sd = 30)))) |>
  ungroup() |>
  mutate(across(c(speaker, l1, traj), factor), l1_o = as.ordered(l1)) |>
  select(speaker, l1, l1_o, traj, duration, time, f2)
contrasts(price$l1_o) <- "contr.treatment"
```

# Dependencies

::: {.fact}
`Did you know:` Prat and colleagues recorded 22 Egyptian fruit bats for 75 days. Their calls carried information about the caller, the context and even the [addressee]{.hl}: the bat the call was directed at.

_Source: Prat, Taub & Yovel (2016), Scientific Reports_
:::

## Four kinds of model

| | Fixed effects only | With random effects |
|:--|:--|:--|
| Parametric terms | LM, `lm()` | LMER, `lmer()` |
| Smooth terms | GAM, `bam()` | GAMM, `bam()` |

. . .

In `{mgcv}`, random effects are written as smooth terms, so the same function fits GAMs and GAMMs.

## Two levels of dependency

- Neighbouring measurements of the same token are more similar than measurements far apart: dependency within a [trajectory]{.hl}
- The 110 measurements of a speaker share that speaker's vocal tract and habits: dependency within a [speaker]{.hl}, and in real data within a word too

Lecture 4's model ignored both, so its confidence intervals were too narrow.

## Residual autocorrelation {.smaller}

```{r}
resid_acf <- function(res, traj, max_lag = 8) {
  d <- tibble(res, traj)
  map(0:max_lag, \(l) d |>
    mutate(res_lag = lag(res, l), .by = traj) |>
    summarise(acf = cor(res, res_lag, use = "complete.obs")) |>
    mutate(lag = l)) |>
    list_rbind()
}
m_gam <- bam(f2 ~ l1_o + s(time, k = 10) + s(time, by = l1_o, k = 10),
             data = price, method = "ML")
acf_gam <- resid_acf(residuals(m_gam), price$traj)
```

The [autocorrelation]{.hl} at lag 1 is the correlation between each residual and the residual one measurement earlier in the same trajectory; lag 2 skips one measurement, and so on. `itsadug::acf_resid()` does the same with base `R` graphics.

## Residual autocorrelation

```{r, fig.height = 2.5}
ggplot(acf_gam, aes(x = lag, y = acf)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = muted) +
  geom_segment(aes(xend = lag, yend = 0), colour = kingfisher, linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_point(colour = kingfisher, size = 3) +
  labs(x = "Lag (measurements)", y = "Autocorrelation")
```

Neighbouring residuals correlate at about `r round(acf_gam$acf[2], 2)`, and the correlation is still clearly positive several measurements apart.

# Random effects in GAMMs

::: {.fact}
`Did you know:` fruit bat pups raised without hearing adult bats kept producing underdeveloped, [pup-like]{.hl} calls far into adolescence.

_Source: Prat, Taub & Yovel (2015), Science Advances_
:::

## Three kinds of random effect

| `{mgcv}` term | Random effect |
|:--|:--|
| `s(speaker, bs = "re")` | random intercepts by speaker |
| `s(speaker, time, bs = "re")` | random slopes over time by speaker |
| `s(time, speaker, bs = "fs", m = 1)` | random smooths over time by speaker |

. . .

Watch the order: random slopes put the grouping factor first, random smooths put the continuous predictor first.

## Fitting the three {.smaller}

```{r}
m_int <- bam(f2 ~ l1_o + s(time, k = 10) + s(time, by = l1_o, k = 10) +
               s(speaker, bs = "re"),
             data = price, method = "ML")
m_slope <- bam(f2 ~ l1_o + s(time, k = 10) + s(time, by = l1_o, k = 10) +
                 s(speaker, bs = "re") + s(speaker, time, bs = "re"),
               data = price, method = "ML")
m_smooth <- bam(f2 ~ l1_o + s(time, k = 10) + s(time, by = l1_o, k = 10) +
                  s(time, speaker, bs = "fs", m = 1, k = 5),
                data = price, method = "ML")
```

## What each one allows

```{r speaker-fits, echo = FALSE, fig.height = 3.6}
speaker_grid <- distinct(price, speaker, l1, l1_o) |>
  crossing(time = seq(0, 100, by = 2))
list(`Random intercepts` = m_int, `+ random slopes` = m_slope, `Random smooths` = m_smooth) |>
  imap(\(m, name) mutate(speaker_grid, fit = as.numeric(predict(m, speaker_grid)), model = name)) |>
  list_rbind() |>
  mutate(model = fct_inorder(model)) |>
  ggplot(aes(time, fit, group = speaker, colour = l1)) +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.8) +
  facet_wrap(~ model) +
  labs(x = "Time (%)", y = "Fitted F2 (Hz)", colour = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "right")
```

One line per speaker. Intercepts shift each speaker's curve up or down, slopes tilt it, and random smooths let each speaker's curve take its own shape.

## Random smooths

- `bs = "fs"` fits one smooth per speaker, with a [shared smoothing parameter]{.hl}, much like random slopes share one variance
- `m = 1` changes the penalty so that each speaker's smooth is pulled toward a flat line, as a random effect should be (Sóskuthy, 2017)
- `k` applies to each speaker: 20 speakers with `k = 5` add 100 coefficients. Keep `k` low; too many coefficients for the data stops the model with an error
- Many levels make random smooths slow and memory-hungry

## The random slope equivalent

- Our groups differ [between]{.hl} speakers: each speaker is English or Italian, so the difference smooth cannot vary by speaker
- When a comparison is [within]{.hl} speakers, say two vowels from every speaker, the model also needs speakers to differ in the vowel difference, like a by-speaker random slope in `lmer()`


One way is a random smooth for every speaker and vowel combination, `s(time, speaker_vowel, bs = "fs", m = 1)`. Sóskuthy (2021) compares this and other options in simulations.

# Autocorrelation

::: {.fact}
`Did you know:` isolated fruit bat pups that heard recordings of adult bats developed a repertoire that [copied]{.hl} the playbacks.

_Source: Prat, Taub & Yovel (2015), Science Advances_
:::

## Two solutions

Random smooths by speaker handle dependencies within speakers. For the dependencies within each trajectory, there are two options:

- [Random smooths by trajectory]{.hl}, `s(time, traj, bs = "fs", m = 1)`, give each of the 200 tokens its own smooth
- An [AR1 error model]{.hl} predicts the error at each measurement partly from the error at the previous one, with the correlation `rho`

## An AR1 model {.smaller}

```{r}
m_noar <- bam(f2 ~ l1_o + s(time, k = 10) + s(time, by = l1_o, k = 10) +
                s(time, speaker, bs = "fs", m = 1, k = 5),
              data = price, method = "ML")
rho <- itsadug::start_value_rho(m_noar)
m_ar <- bam(f2 ~ l1_o + s(time, k = 10) + s(time, by = l1_o, k = 10) +
              s(time, speaker, bs = "fs", m = 1, k = 5),
            data = price, method = "ML", AR.start = price$time == 0, rho = rho)
```

- `start_value_rho()` estimates `rho` from the lag-1 autocorrelation of a model without the AR1 component
- `AR.start` marks the first measurement of each trajectory, so the error model does not link one token to the next. The data must be sorted by trajectory and time

## Did it work?

```{r acf-compare, echo = FALSE, fig.height = 3.3}
list(`GAM, no random effects` = residuals(m_gam),
     `Random smooths by speaker` = residuals(m_noar),
     `+ AR1` = m_ar$std.rsd) |>
  imap(\(r, name) mutate(resid_acf(r, price$traj), model = name)) |>
  list_rbind() |>
  mutate(model = fct_inorder(model)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = lag, y = acf)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = muted) +
  geom_segment(aes(xend = lag, yend = 0), colour = kingfisher, linewidth = 1.1) +
  geom_point(colour = kingfisher, size = 2.5) +
  facet_wrap(~ model) +
  labs(x = "Lag (measurements)", y = "Autocorrelation")
```

For the AR1 model, the autocorrelation is computed on the [standardised residuals]{.hl}, `m_ar$std.rsd`, which take the error model into account.

## Random smooths or AR1?

- Random smooths by trajectory become very slow with many trajectories: Sóskuthy (2018) puts the practical limit at around 500 to 800
- AR1 adds almost no computing time, so for large data sets it is the only option
- An AR1 model may not remove all autocorrelation for some kinds of curves: always check the residuals
- `rho` is shared by all trajectories, and in `{mgcv}` the AR1 option is available in `bam()` only

# Non-linear interactions

::: {.fact}
`Did you know:` fruit bat pups raised in three groups, each hearing a different playback, developed distinct [dialects]{.hl} from about six months of age, each closer to its own playback.

_Source: Prat, Azoulay, Dor & Yovel (2017), PLoS Biology_
:::

## Duration and shape {.smaller}

```{r, fig.height = 2.7}
ggplot(price, aes(x = time, y = f2, group = traj, colour = duration)) +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.6) +
  scale_colour_viridis_c(option = "magma", begin = 0.2) +
  facet_wrap(~ l1) +
  labs(x = "Time (%)", y = "F2 (Hz)", colour = "Duration (ms)") +
  theme(legend.position = "right")
```

Short vowels (dark) stop lower: the glide [undershoots]{.hl} its target. Duration changes the shape of the curve as well as its height.

## `s()`, `te()` and `ti()`

- `s(duration)` adds a smooth effect of duration on overall F2: it can shift whole curves, but not change their shape
- `te(time, duration)` is a [tensor product smooth]{.hl}: one surface over time and duration, including both main effects
- `ti(time, duration)` is the [tensor product interaction]{.hl} alone. Combined with `s(time)` and `s(duration)`, it separates the main effects from the interaction, so each gets its own row in the summary

## The model {.smaller}

```{r}
m_dur <- bam(f2 ~ l1_o + s(time, k = 10) + s(time, by = l1_o, k = 10) +
               s(duration) + ti(time, duration) +
               s(time, speaker, bs = "fs", m = 1, k = 5),
             data = price, method = "ML", AR.start = price$time == 0, rho = rho)
round(summary(m_dur)$s.table, 2)
```

## Predictions at three durations {.smaller}

```{r, fig.height = 2.7}
predict_gam(m_dur, series = "time", length_out = 50,
            values = list(duration = c(150, 220, 290)),
            exclude_terms = "s(time,speaker)") |>
  ggplot(aes(x = time, y = f2, colour = factor(duration), fill = factor(duration))) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lower_ci, ymax = upper_ci), alpha = 0.2, colour = NA) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.2) +
  facet_wrap(~ l1_o) +
  labs(x = "Time (%)", y = "Predicted F2 (Hz)", colour = "Duration (ms)", fill = "Duration (ms)") +
  theme(legend.position = "right")
```

`exclude_terms` removes the random smooths, so the curves are for an [average speaker]{.hl}.

## The surface {.smaller}

```{r, fig.height = 2.6}
predict_gam(m_dur, series = c("time", "duration"), length_out = 40,
            values = list(l1_o = "English"), exclude_terms = "s(time,speaker)") |>
  ggplot(aes(x = time, y = duration, fill = f2, z = f2)) +
  geom_raster() +
  geom_contour(colour = floor_col, alpha = 0.6, bins = 8) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "mako", begin = 0.15) +
  labs(x = "Time (%)", y = "Duration (ms)", fill = "Predicted\nF2 (Hz)") +
  theme(legend.position = "right")
```

A heat map shows the whole interaction for English speakers, but prediction curves at a few durations are easier to read.

# Checking and reporting

::: {.fact}
`Did you know:` the pups in the dialect experiment heard their mothers too, but their calls moved toward the playback of the whole colony. Prat and colleagues called this [crowd vocal learning]{.hl}.

_Source: Prat, Azoulay, Dor & Yovel (2017), PLoS Biology_
:::

## Checking the model {.smaller}

```{r}
k.check(m_dur)
```

```{r, fig.height = 2.1}
p_resid <- ggplot(tibble(fitted = fitted(m_dur), res = m_dur$std.rsd), aes(fitted, res)) +
  geom_point(colour = kingfisher, alpha = 0.2) + labs(x = "Fitted F2 (Hz)", y = "Std. residual")
p_qq <- ggplot(tibble(res = m_dur$std.rsd), aes(sample = res)) +
  geom_qq(colour = kingfisher, alpha = 0.4) + geom_qq_line(colour = mist) + labs(x = "Theoretical", y = "Sample")
p_resid + p_qq
```

## Testing the group difference {.smaller}

```{r}
m_dur_null <- bam(f2 ~ s(time, k = 10) + s(duration) + ti(time, duration) +
                    s(time, speaker, bs = "fs", m = 1, k = 5),
                  data = price, method = "ML", AR.start = price$time == 0, rho = rho)
itsadug::compareML(m_dur_null, m_dur)
```

Both models have the same random effects, error model and `rho`, and are fitted with `method = "ML"`.

## GAM versus GAMM {.smaller}

```{r, fig.height = 2.0}
compare <- list(l1_o = c("Italian", "English"))
bind_rows(`GAM (lecture 4)` = as_tibble(get_difference(m_gam, "time", compare, length_out = 50)),
          `GAMM with AR1` = as_tibble(get_difference(m_dur, "time", compare, length_out = 50,
                                                     exclude_terms = "s(time,speaker)")),
          .id = "model") |>
  ggplot(aes(x = time, y = diff, colour = model, fill = model)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = muted, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lower_ci, ymax = upper_ci), alpha = 0.25, colour = NA) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.1) +
  labs(x = "Time (%)", y = "Italian − English F2 (Hz)", colour = NULL, fill = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "right")
```

The GAM treats the 2,200 measurements as independent; the GAMM knows they come from 200 tokens and 20 speakers.

## Reporting {.smaller}

> We fitted a GAMM to F2 (`bam()`, `{mgcv}`; Wood, 2017) with an ordered factor for L1 (reference: English), a reference smooth over time, a difference smooth for Italian speakers, a smooth for duration and a tensor product interaction between time and duration. Random smooths over time by speaker (`m = 1`, `k = 5`) and an AR1 error model (ρ = `r round(rho, 2)`) accounted for dependencies within speakers and trajectories.

. . .

Then report the model comparison, and show the prediction curves and the difference smooth with their confidence intervals.

## Summary

::: {.takeaway}
- Curve data have dependencies within trajectories and within speakers (and words); ignoring them makes intervals too narrow
- In `{mgcv}`, random intercepts and slopes use `bs = "re"`, and [random smooths]{.hl} use `bs = "fs"` with `m = 1`
- An [AR1 error model]{.hl} handles autocorrelation within trajectories cheaply; check the standardised residuals
- `ti()` adds a [non-linear interaction]{.hl} between two continuous predictors; show it with prediction curves at a few values
- Test effects by comparing ML-fitted models with the same random effects and error model
:::
